title: Designing for Users: UX and Accessibility

pages.c11-p01: Explain what user-centred design is and why products that work can still fail their users
pages.c11-p02: Describe how designers find out user needs through interviews, surveys and observation, and use personas
pages.c11-p03: Write user stories in the form 'As a …, I want …, so that …' with acceptance criteria to plan what a product must do
pages.c11-p04: Describe usability principles such as consistency, feedback, simple navigation and error prevention, using good and bad examples
pages.c11-p05: Explain how wireframes and prototypes, from paper sketches to high-fidelity models, use abstraction to test ideas before building
pages.c11-p06: Explain what accessibility is, who it helps, and how the WCAG guidelines and the POUR principles guide accessible design
pages.c11-p07: Explain inclusive design and how bias can leave users out, considering different ages, abilities, languages and devices
pages.c11-p08: Describe how to test a design with users, including think-aloud testing and A/B tests, and use the results to improve it
pages.c11-p09: Describe development cycles and compare the waterfall approach with iterative and agile approaches
pages.c11-p10: Apply user-centred design to a case study: redesigning a school canteen ordering website

q.q: What is the main idea of user-centred design?
o: The latest technology is used at every stage
The needs of the users come first at every stage
The designer's own taste guides every stage
The cheapest option is chosen at every stage
q.why: User-centred design puts the people who will use the product at the centre of every decision.

q.q: Which term means how the whole experience of using a product feels to the user?
o: User experience (UX)
User interface (UI)
Usability testing
User story
q.why: UX is about how the whole experience feels: easy and pleasant, or frustrating.

q.q: A designer changes the size and position of the Order button. Which part of the product are they working on?
o: The database
The server
The network
The user interface
q.why: The user interface is the part users see and touch, such as buttons.

q.q: A homework app passes every test the programmer runs, but most pupils give up trying to upload work. What is the best description?
o: It is a success because all the tests were passed
It has a coding bug that the tests have missed
It works, but it does not work well for its users
The pupils need to be trained to use it properly
q.why: Working code is not enough: the design has failed the people it was built for.

q.q: Which question best sums up the thinking behind user-centred design?
o: How fast does this code run?
Who does this design work for?
How many features can we add?
Which language should we use?
q.why: User-centred design asks who a design works for, not just whether it works.

q.q: Which is the most likely reason a product fails its users?
o: The team guessed what users wanted instead of asking
The team tested early versions with real users
The team used simple words on the buttons
The team kept the number of features small
q.why: Guessing instead of finding out real needs is a common cause of failure; the others are good practice.

q.q: A car park machine only accepts payment through a phone app. Which group is it most likely to fail?
o: Drivers who park for a short time
Drivers who already have the app installed
Drivers who visit the car park every day
Drivers without a smartphone or mobile signal
q.why: A design that relies on one way of paying leaves out people who cannot use that method.

q.q: Why is a designer a poor choice to be the only tester of their own app?
o: They are not allowed to see the app before it is released
They will always find too many problems to fix in time
They know how it works, so they will not struggle like a new user
They cannot use the app on a phone during development
q.why: The designer already knows where everything is, so they cannot see the problems new users meet.

q.q: Which word describes how easily a user can complete a task with a product?
o: Accessibility
Usability
Fidelity
Iteration
q.why: Usability is how easy it is to use a product to get a job done.

q.q: A pupil keeps pushing a door that has to be pulled. According to user-centred design, whose fault is this mainly?
o: The door's designer, because the design gives the wrong clue
The pupil, because they should read the sign more carefully
The school, because it should have trained every pupil
Nobody, because doors are always confusing to some people
q.why: When people struggle with a product, it usually means the design has let them down.

q.q: Which research method is best for getting quick answers from hundreds of people?
o: Interview
Observation
Focus group
Survey
q.why: Surveys can be sent to many people and the answers counted easily.

q.q: Which research method gives the most detail about why a user feels a certain way?
o: Survey
A/B test
Interview
Wireframe
q.why: Interviews allow open questions and follow-ups, so you learn the reasons behind answers.

q.q: What is the main advantage of observation as a research method?
o: It collects answers from a very large number of people
It shows what people actually do, not just what they say
It is the quickest method because no notes are needed
It lets users explain their reasons in their own words
q.why: Watching people reveals real behaviour, which can differ from what they report.

q.q: Which of these is primary research for a new canteen app?
o: Watching pupils in the lunch queue
Reading a news article about school meals
Looking at government statistics on phones
Reading reviews of other canteen apps
q.why: Primary research is collected yourself, directly from users.

q.q: Which interview question would give the designer the most useful information?
o: Do you like eating in the school canteen?
Is the new lunch app good or bad?
Have you ever used the lunch app?
Tell me about the last time you ordered lunch
q.why: Open questions invite detailed answers instead of a simple yes or no.

q.q: Orla, 12, Year 8, has an old phone and wants to order lunch before first period. The design team made her up from their research. What is Orla?
o: A user story
A tester
A persona
A stakeholder
q.why: A persona is a realistic made-up character based on research into a group of users.

q.q: Which of these would you NOT normally include in a persona?
o: The person's goals when using the app
The programming language the app will use
The devices the person uses
The things that frustrate the person
q.why: A persona describes the user, not the technology used to build the product.

q.q: A survey says 90% of pupils read the menu before ordering, but observation shows most just copy their friends. What should the designer conclude?
o: What people say and do can differ, so use more than one method
The survey must be correct because more people took part
The observation must be wrong because only a few were watched
Pupils should be told to read the menu before ordering
q.why: Using several methods gives a truer picture, because reported and real behaviour often differ.

q.q: Why is creating a persona an example of abstraction?
o: It turns the users' answers into program code for the app
It removes all the details so that every user looks the same
It hides the real names of users so their data stays private
It keeps the important details of many users and leaves out the rest
q.why: Abstraction means keeping what matters and removing unnecessary detail.

q.q: A designer writes a persona saying 'older people cannot use computers' without doing any research. What is wrong with this?
o: Personas should never include a user's age
Older people should not be included in personas
It is a stereotype, not based on research into real users
Personas must always be written after the app is built
q.why: Personas must come from real research; many older people are confident users.

q.q: Which is the correct template for a user story?
o: If [condition], then [action], else [action]
As a [user], I want [goal], so that [reason]
Input [data], process [data], output [data]
Given [start], when [event], then [result]
q.why: User stories use As a..., I want..., so that....

q.q: In 'As a parent, I want a text when the balance is low, so that my child never misses lunch', who is the user?
o: A parent
A child
The canteen
The school
q.why: The user comes after 'As a'.

q.q: In 'As a player, I want to save my game, so that I can carry on later', what is the goal?
o: To be a player
To carry on later
To win the game
To save the game
q.why: The goal comes after 'I want'; carrying on later is the reason.

q.q: What is the purpose of the 'so that' part of a user story?
o: It names the type of user who wants it
It lists the tests the feature must pass
It explains why the user needs the feature
It says how long the feature will take
q.why: The 'so that' gives the reason or benefit, which helps the team design it well.

q.q: 'The confirmation shows the order number, the food and the collection time.' What is this an example of?
o: A user story
An acceptance criterion
A persona
A wireframe
q.why: It is a specific, testable check that shows a user story is complete.

q.q: Why is 'The page loads fast' a weak acceptance criterion?
o: It has no measurement, so it cannot be tested with a clear yes or no
It is too short to be written down as an acceptance criterion
It is about speed, and acceptance criteria cannot mention speed
It should have been written as a user story instead
q.why: A strong criterion is measurable, e.g. loads in under 3 seconds on a phone.

q.q: What is wrong with the story 'As a developer, I want to use a cloud database, so that data is stored'?
o: It is missing the 'so that' part
It does not say which type of user
It has too many parts to be a story
It is about the technology, not what a user wants
q.why: Good user stories describe what a real user wants to achieve.

q.q: Orla says: 'I never know if my order has gone through.' Which user story best captures her need?
o: As a pupil, I want more food on the menu, so that I have more choice
As a pupil, I want a faster server, so that the database is updated
As a pupil, I want a confirmation after ordering, so that I know my lunch will be ready
As a canteen worker, I want an order list, so that I can cook enough
q.why: Her problem is not knowing if the order worked, so she needs a confirmation.

q.q: How do user stories help a team decide what to build first?
o: The longest stories are always built first
Stories can be put in order and the most important built first
Every story is built at the same time
Stories are built in alphabetical order
q.why: Teams prioritise stories so the most valuable features come first.

q.q: Which of these is a nice-to-have story that could wait for a later version of a canteen app?
o: As a pupil, I want to rate today's lunch, so that the canteen knows what I liked
As a pupil, I want to pay for my lunch, so that I can collect it
As a pupil, I want to see the menu, so that I can choose what to eat
As a pupil, I want a confirmation, so that I know my order worked
q.why: The other stories are essential for ordering; rating lunch is useful but not essential.

q.q: You tap Pay and nothing happens, so you tap again and pay twice. Which usability principle was missing?
o: Consistency
Abstraction
Fidelity
Feedback
q.why: The app should have shown straight away that the payment was being processed.

q.q: The Save button is blue at the top on one screen and grey at the bottom on the next. Which principle is broken?
o: Feedback
Error prevention
Consistency
Accessibility
q.why: Things that do the same job should look and behave the same everywhere.

q.q: A form asks for your year group. Which design prevents the most errors?
o: A free text box with no hint
A drop-down list of Years 8 to 14
A free text box with an example
A message if you type it wrongly
q.why: Choosing from a list makes it impossible to type an invalid year group.

q.q: Which three things should a good error message tell the user?
o: What went wrong, why, and what to do next
The error code, the time and the server name
Who caused it, when, and how to report it
What went wrong, the code, and a help link
q.why: Plain words about what, why and what next help users recover.

q.q: Where should an error message about a form box appear?
o: In a pop-up after the whole page reloads
At the very top of a long page
On a separate help page
Right next to the box that needs fixing
q.why: Placing it beside the problem helps users find and fix it quickly.

q.q: Which button label best follows 'speak the user's language' on a shopping app?
o: Execute transaction
Submit payload
Pay now
Process request
q.why: Use plain words users already know instead of technical jargon.

q.q: Why do good apps show a list of recent searches?
o: Lists use less memory than text boxes
Recognising something is easier than recalling it
It makes the app load more quickly
It stops users making any spelling errors
q.why: Choosing from a list (recognition) is easier than remembering and typing (recall).

q.q: A form wipes everything you typed because one box was wrong. Which is the best fix?
o: Keep what was typed and show the problem next to that box
Show a bigger red warning at the top of the page
Add a Clear button so users can start again quickly
Ask users to check every box carefully before sending
q.why: Users should be helped to recover from errors without losing their work.

q.q: Which of these is an example of good navigation in an app?
o: Twelve menu items with fun made-up names
A menu that is hidden until you shake the phone
A menu that changes order depending on the page
A few clearly named menu items that stay in the same place
q.why: Simple, clearly named, consistent menus help users know where they are and how to move around.

q.q: A designer says: 'The screen looks amazing, so it must be easy to use.' What is the flaw in this argument?
o: Attractive designs are always harder to use
Usability can only be judged by programmers
Looking good and being usable are different things
Good-looking screens always load slowly
q.why: A beautiful design can still have tiny text, hidden menus or confusing steps.

q.q: On a quiz app, after pressing Submit the screen goes blank, the menu then moves to the bottom, and an error says 'NullReferenceException'. Which principles are broken, in that order?
o: Consistency, feedback, error prevention
Feedback, consistency, speak the user's language
Error prevention, feedback, consistency
Feedback, error prevention, consistency
q.why: A blank screen gives no feedback, a moving menu breaks consistency and the message is jargon.

q.q: A pupil draws plain boxes labelled 'menu', 'logo' and 'image' to plan a home page. What have they drawn?
o: A wireframe
A persona
A user story
A storyboard
q.why: A wireframe is a simple layout plan using boxes and labels.

q.q: What is a prototype?
o: The final version of a product sold to customers
A list of all the features a product will have
A document describing the users of a product
An early model of a product that users can try out
q.why: Prototypes let designers test ideas before the real product is built.

q.q: What does low fidelity mean?
o: Detailed and very close to the real thing
Tested by only a small number of users
Simple and rough, like a paper sketch
Built using a slow internet connection
q.why: Fidelity describes how detailed and realistic a prototype is.

q.q: A team has a clickable model with real colours, fonts and photos, but no real data behind it. What is it?
o: A low-fidelity prototype
A high-fidelity prototype
A wireframe
The finished product
q.why: It looks and feels like the real app but is still a model for testing.

q.q: Why do teams usually start with low-fidelity prototypes?
o: They are quick and cheap, so big changes cost little
They look more professional to show to customers
They can be sold to users before the real app
They contain code that is reused in the final app
q.why: Fixing problems on paper early is far cheaper than fixing finished software.

q.q: Why do wireframes leave out colours, images and real text?
o: Because colours cannot be shown in design software
Because images would make the wireframe too slow
To make the wireframe accessible to blind users
To focus on the layout, which is a form of abstraction
q.why: Removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters is abstraction.

q.q: In a wireframe, what does a box with an X drawn through it usually mean?
o: This part has been deleted
This button closes the app
An image will go here
This part has an error
q.why: A crossed box is the usual placeholder for an image.

q.q: What feedback are users most likely to give on a high-fidelity prototype that they would not give on a paper sketch?
o: Comments on whether they can find the main features
Comments on small details such as the shade of a button
Comments on the order in which screens appear
Comments on whether the app does what they need
q.why: Realistic prototypes draw attention to details; rough sketches keep the focus on big ideas.

q.q: In a paper prototype test, the tester keeps tapping the food photo instead of the small Add button. What should the team do?
o: Redraw the screen so tapping the food item adds it
Tell the tester to tap the Add button instead
Wait until the real app is built to fix it
Ignore it because paper tests are not realistic
q.why: The test has revealed a real problem, so change the design and retest.

q.q: A team spends a week on a beautiful high-fidelity design, then testing shows users find the order of screens confusing. What lesson does this show?
o: High-fidelity designs should never be user tested
Users cannot judge the order of screens fairly
Visual design is more important than screen order
Sketch and test the layout first, then add polish
q.why: Starting with low fidelity avoids wasting time polishing a layout that may be wrong.

q.q: What does WCAG stand for?
o: World Computer Accessibility Group
Website Colour and Graphics Guide
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
Web Coding Access Grades
q.why: WCAG is the international standard for accessible web content.

q.q: Which organisation publishes WCAG?
o: The BBC (British Broadcasting Corporation)
The W3C (World Wide Web Consortium)
CCEA (the exam board for Northern Ireland)
The NHS (National Health Service)
q.why: The W3C also sets the standards for HTML and CSS.

q.q: What do the letters POUR stand for?
o: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust
Perceivable, Organised, Usable, Readable
Private, Operable, Useful, Reliable
Predictable, Open, Understandable, Responsive
q.why: WCAG is organised under these four principles.

q.q: Which WCAG level is the usual target for websites?
o: Level A
Level AAA
No level: WCAG has one set of rules
Level AA
q.why: A is the minimum, AAA the highest; AA is the usual target, including for UK public sector sites.

q.q: What is alt text?
o: Text that appears when you hover over a button
A different font used when the main one fails
A description of an image that a screen reader reads aloud
Text that changes colour when it is selected
q.why: Alt text lets people who cannot see an image know what it shows.

q.q: Captions on a video mainly support which POUR principle?
o: Operable
Perceivable
Understandable
Robust
q.why: Captions let deaf users perceive what is said.

q.q: Making every button work with the Tab and Enter keys mainly supports which POUR principle?
o: Operable
Perceivable
Robust
Understandable
q.why: Operable means users can use every control, including without a mouse.

q.q: Writing correct, standard HTML so it works with lots of browsers and screen readers supports which POUR principle?
o: Operable
Perceivable
Understandable
Robust
q.why: Robust content works with many technologies, including assistive ones.

q.q: What contrast ratio does WCAG AA require for normal-sized text?
o: At least 2 : 1
At least 3 : 1
At least 4.5 : 1
At least 7 : 1
q.why: AA needs 4.5 : 1 for normal text; 3 : 1 is for large text and 7 : 1 is the AAA level.

q.q: A pupil has a broken wrist in a cast for six weeks. What type of accessibility need is this?
o: Permanent
Temporary
Situational
Perceivable
q.why: It will go away when the wrist heals, so it is temporary.

q.q: A canteen website marks vegetarian dishes only by colouring them green. Why is this a problem?
o: Colour-blind users may not be able to tell which dishes are green
Green text cannot be shown on most mobile phone screens
Screen readers read green text more slowly than black
Green text breaks the consistency of the menu page
q.why: Never rely on colour alone; add a label such as (V).

q.q: Which alt text is best for a photo of the school rugby team holding a trophy?
o: image.jpg
Image of a photo of a picture
Click here to see the photo
School rugby team holding the cup after the final
q.why: Good alt text briefly describes what matters in the image.

q.q: A team designs an app that works for older users, new arrivals learning English and pupils on slow phones. What is this called?
o: Abstraction
Waterfall design
Inclusive design
A/B testing
q.why: Inclusive design means designing for the full range of people who might use a product.

q.q: What is bias in the design of a product?
o: When it shows adverts for products the user might like
When it works well for some groups but badly for others
When it is tested by more than one group of users
When the designer prefers one colour scheme to another
q.why: Bias means some groups are served worse than others, usually by accident.

q.q: A sign-up form rejects the surname O'Neill. What is the most likely cause?
o: The form only accepts letters, not apostrophes
The user typed the name into the wrong box
Surnames over five letters are not allowed
The website has been hacked by criminals
q.why: The programmer assumed names only use the letters A to Z.

q.q: An all-teenage design team builds an app with tiny text and swipe-only menus. Older users struggle. What is the best explanation?
o: Older users did not read the instructions
Tiny text is required on mobile phones
Swipe menus are banned for older users
The team designed for people like themselves
q.why: Bias often happens when designers assume users are like them.

q.q: Which choice best includes families who speak another language at home?
o: Longer sentences that explain everything in detail
More pictures with no words underneath them
Plain English, labelled icons and a translation option
A separate website only in the other language
q.why: Simple language, clear icons with labels and translation help the widest range of users.

q.q: Which design choice best includes users in rural areas with poor mobile signal?
o: Autoplay a welcome video on every page
Keep pages small so they load quickly
Use the largest, sharpest images available
Require the very latest version of the app
q.why: Light pages work on slow or limited connections.

q.q: A face-recognition system works much better for some groups of people than others. What is the most likely reason?
o: Its training data contained mostly photos of some groups
Some groups of people are harder for cameras to see
Face recognition only works in very bright light
The system was tested too many times before release
q.why: Systems that learn from data can be biased if the data is not varied.

q.q: What is the best way for a team to reduce bias in their product?
o: Ask the design team to test it more carefully
Add more features so everyone finds something
Use the newest and most powerful technology
Research and test with a wide range of real users
q.why: Including a varied range of users reveals problems the team would not notice.

q.q: A school app shows every pupil's live location to their friends. Which inclusive-design question does this most raise?
o: Will this feature load quickly enough?
Does this feature use enough colours?
Who might be put at risk by this feature?
Can this feature work on a laptop?
q.why: Inclusive design also asks who might be harmed, not only who is left out.

q.q: What is usability testing?
o: Checking the code for spelling mistakes
Watching real users try to complete real tasks
Running the app on a very fast computer
Asking the designer to list the features
q.why: Usability testing observes real users to find problems with the design.

q.q: A tester says, 'I'm looking for the basket... maybe it's this icon... no, that's my account.' What kind of test is this?
o: Think-aloud testing
A/B testing
A survey
A focus group
q.why: In think-aloud testing users say what they are thinking as they go.

q.q: During a test, a pupil cannot find the Pay button. What should the person running the test do?
o: Point at the button to save time
End the test and choose a new tester
Tell them they are doing it wrong
Note the problem and let them keep trying
q.why: Helping hides the problem; if users need help, the design needs changing.

q.q: A website shows half its visitors a red Buy button and half a green one, then counts sales. What is this?
o: A think-aloud test
An interview
An A/B test
An observation
q.why: Two versions shown to different groups and compared is an A/B test.

q.q: What can an A/B test NOT tell you on its own?
o: Which version worked better
Why one version worked better
How many users used each version
How many users completed the task
q.why: For the why, you need to watch and listen to users, e.g. think-aloud testing.

q.q: Version A: 120 orders from 400 visitors. Version B: 200 orders from 400 visitors. What is Version B's success rate?
4 out of 5 testers completed a task. What is the task success rate?
Which usability problem should be fixed first?
o: One tester would like a different shade of blue
Two testers would like to have a dark mode
Four out of five testers cannot complete the order
One tester thinks the logo is a little small
q.why: Fix serious problems that affect the most users first.

q.q: Testing with about how many users usually reveals most of the biggest usability problems?
o: About 50
About 5
About 500
About 5,000
q.why: A small test with around five users finds most big problems; then fix and test again.

q.q: Why should a team test again after changing a design?
o: To check the fix worked and has not caused a new problem
Because the first test results are always deleted
Because users forget what they said in the first test
To make the testing stage take up more of the time
q.why: Retesting confirms that the change improved things.

q.q: In the waterfall approach, how are the stages carried out?
o: All stages at the same time
In short loops repeated many times
In any order the team prefers
Each stage once, fully, in order
q.why: Waterfall flows down through the stages once, like water down steps.

q.q: An agile team spends two weeks building and testing the three most important user stories, then shows users. What is that two-week block called?
o: A waterfall
A persona
A sprint
A prototype
q.why: In agile, work is done in short fixed blocks called sprints.

q.q: How long does a sprint usually last?
o: One to four hours
One to four weeks
One to four months
One to four years
q.why: Sprints are short so users can give feedback often.

q.q: A team builds version 1, tests it, improves it to version 2, tests again, then makes version 3. What is this way of working called?
o: Iterative
Waterfall
Abstraction
Linear
q.why: Going round the cycle repeatedly, improving each time, is iterative development.

q.q: What is the main disadvantage of waterfall for a brand-new app?
o: It does not include any testing stage at all
Users see the app too often during the project
It can only be used by very small teams
Users may not see it until near the end, when changes are costly
q.why: Problems with the design are found late, when they are expensive to fix.

q.q: Which project is best suited to an agile approach?
o: Software with exact rules fixed by law
Copying an existing system exactly
A new app where users' needs are still unclear
A program that will never need changes
q.why: Agile handles uncertain or changing needs through regular feedback.

q.q: Which project is best suited to the waterfall approach?
o: A new social app for pupils with uncertain features
Traffic light software with fixed, safety-critical rules
A game where players' feedback will shape new levels
A school app whose features may change each term
q.why: Waterfall suits clear, fixed requirements that must be fully planned and tested first.

q.q: Which statement about agile is a misconception?
o: Agile means there is no planning
Agile teams test every version
Agile welcomes changing needs
Agile shows users working versions often
q.why: Agile teams plan carefully, just in smaller pieces.

q.q: Which is the correct order of the waterfall stages?
o: Design, analysis, testing, implementation, deployment
Analysis, implementation, design, testing, deployment
Implementation, analysis, design, deployment, testing
Analysis, design, implementation, testing, deployment
q.why: You find out requirements, design, build, test, then release.

q.q: Why does agile fit well with user-centred design?
o: Agile projects do not need any users at all
Agile always produces higher-fidelity designs
Users test working versions after every sprint
Agile skips the research stage to save time
q.why: Regular user feedback shapes each new sprint.

q.q: In the canteen case study, what was the first step the design team took?
o: Choosing colours and fonts for the new website
Researching user needs with surveys, interviews and observation
Writing the code for the new ordering page
Launching the new website to every pupil
q.why: User-centred design starts by finding out what users need.

q.q: Research showed most pupils use phones, but the old site was designed for laptops. Which change follows from this?
o: Design for phones first, and make it work on laptops too
Ask pupils to use the school laptops to order lunch
Make the text smaller so more fits on the screen
Remove the website and take orders on paper only
q.why: Design for the devices your users actually use.

q.q: 3 out of 5 testers could not find the basket. After a redesign, 5 out of 5 found it. What was the success rate before and after?
o: 60% before and 100% after
30% before and 50% after
3% before and 5% after
40% before and 100% after
